I. The Supreme Court judgement on the right to menstrual hygiene as an integral part of the
constitutional right to life and dignity provides a long-desired direction towards destigmatising
an essential bodily function and ensuring basic care. While observing that the lack of basic
facilities and the stigma around menstruation directly affect girls’ health, education and privacy,
the bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and R Mahadevan directed all states and Union territories
to ensure within three months that every school has gender-segregated toilets, and
biodegradable or reusable sanitary pads are provided for free to adolescent girls along with safe
disposal facilities. The court also asked the governments to incorporate gender-responsive
curriculums in schools and train the staff in assisting menstruating pupils.
The apex court’s judgement and directions expose the socio-cultural and religious taboos
perpetuated by patriarchal norms. Period shame is every girl’s burden. The event of puberty, a
milestone in human physiological evolution, is celebrated in many Indian traditions. But period
ostracisation is so deeply prevalent in many sections that the victims of such misinformed
belief and gender aggression are eventually socialised to become its carriers. The troubling
apportioning of ‘shame’ continues through generations. For girls born into economically
weaker families, sanitary pads are a luxury. Government schools, an ideal place to clear the
misconceptions for both girls and boys, ignore this duty. To aggravate the insensitive attitude,
their administrators often force hapless teenage girls to explain clothes stains as period blood,
stripping them of dignity.
By one estimate, around 2.3 crore girls drop out of school annually on account of lack of
adequate toilets and menstrual provisions. The launch of the Union Health Ministry’s
Menstrual Hygiene Scheme in 2011 was a landmark attempt to destigmatise menstruation by
giving girls aged 10 to 19 subsidised pads and menstrual education. But it left out the adolescent
girls who are out of school. The right to education is as fundamental a right as the right to live
with dignity. With the Supreme Court spelling out the nuances of the constitutional right of
young girls in detail, it’s time to fill the gaps. For that, government and private schools have to
act in a timebound manner. And all three tiers of government have to ensure that awareness of
the right as well as the health basics reach all sections of India—in every generation.
SOURCE:https://www.newindianexpress.com/editorial/2026/Feb/08/menstruation-rights-as-
institutional-assurance

II. There was commotion in Roaring Camp. It could not have been a fight, for in 1850 that was
not novel enough to have called together the entire settlement. The ditches and claims were not
only deserted, but "Tuttle's grocery" had contributed its gamblers, who, it will be remembered,
calmly continued their game the day that French Pete and Kanaka Joe shot each other to death
over the bar in the front room. The whole camp was collected before a rude cabin on the outer
edge of the clearing. Conversation was carried on in a low tone, but the name of a woman was
frequently repeated. It was a name familiar enough in the camp,—"Cherokee Sal."
Perhaps the less said of her the better. She was a coarse and, it is to be feared, a very sinful
woman. But at that time she was the only woman in Roaring Camp, and was just then lying in
sore extremity when she most needed the ministration of her own sex. Dissolute, abandoned,
and irreclaimable, she was yet suffering a martyrdom hard enough to bear even when veiled by
sympathizing womanhood, but now terrible in her loneliness. The primal curse had come to
her in that original isolation which must have made the punishment of the first transgression
so dreadful. It was, perhaps, part of the expiation of her sin that, at a moment when she most
lacked her sex's intuitive tenderness and care, she met only the half-contemptuous faces of her
masculine associates. Yet a few of the spectators were, I think, touched by her sufferings. Sandy
Tipton thought it was "rough on Sal," and, in the contemplation of her condition, for a moment
rose superior to the fact that he had an ace and two bowers in his sleeve.
It will be seen also that the situation was novel. Deaths were by no means uncommon in
Roaring Camp, but a birth was a new thing. People had been dismissed the camp effectively,
finally, and with no possibility of return; but this was the first time that anybody had been
introduced ab initio. Hence the excitement.
"You go in there, Stumpy," said a prominent citizen known as "Kentuck," addressing one of
the loungers. "Go in there, and see what you kin do. You've had experience in them things."
Perhaps there was a fitness in the selection. Stumpy, in other climes, had been the putative head
of two families; in fact, it was owing to some legal informality in these proceedings that
Roaring Camp—a city of refuge—was indebted to his company. The crowd approved the
choice, and Stumpy was wise enough to bow to the majority. The door closed on the extempore
surgeon and midwife, and Roaring Camp sat down outside, smoked its pipe, and awaited the
issue.

III. There is a sudden meltdown across different asset classes around the world—barring
equities, which have escaped the turmoil till now. Silver and gold, which saw a historic rise in
prices in 2025, have come under pressure of late. The price escalation seen last year proved
ephemeral as silver crashed from a peak of $125 an ounce in the last week of January to a low
of $70 before closing around $77.
The virtual currency market is witnessing its share of volatility—a trend not unfamiliar to this
asset class. Bitcoin is down 44 percent since its October peak of $125,000, while Ethereum has
fallen 56 percent from its August peak of $4,800. The sharp rise and fall in bullion and
cryptocurrencies are closely associated with uncertainty around US-led trade policies. At a
granular level, there are specific reasons for the degree of decline in each asset class.
The lack of clarity on their regulatory status has weighed on cryptos even as institutional buying
has picked up. The fall in gold and silver can be linked to the lower uncertainty around US
trade policy than in 2025. Additionally, the US government’s nomination of Kevin Warsh for
the Fed chair has had a cooling effect on bullion. Warsh is expected to be less aggressive with
rate cuts, fuelling bearish sentiment in both gold and silver. This has led to large-scale outflows
from gold and silver exchange-traded funds, further reinforcing the bearish trend.
The unexpected rise in silver prices in 2025 was attributed to a growing demand-supply gap.
Industrial use of silver has been rising, with demand from the solar energy and electronics
sectors soaring. But at these price levels, the supply gap is expected to shrink, with demand for
investment and jewellery likely to fall in 2026. Irrespective of the steady industrial demand for
silver and other metals such as copper, such steep price rises are unsustainable beyond.
Investors who missed the metals rally in 2025 should not expect a similar run in 2026. The
‘irrational’ expectation of an encore from these metals should therefore be viewed with caution.
Silver and copper are not the new gold, nor are virtual currencies. These are volatile asset
classes, and investors should not treat an exceptional run in any of these as the new normal.

IV. The “ultimate answer to life, the universe and everything”, wrote Douglas Adams in The
Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, is “42”. Or, in other words, the product of six and seven.
There’s one minor snag: No one quite knows what the ultimate question is. In much the same
way, it appears, no adult quite knows what “six-seven” — the newest cultural mayfly that
teens around the world, including in India, are dropping like confetti in classrooms,
playgrounds and at the dining table — means. That is the entire point.
Neologisms of such variety have always marked the boundaries of youth — encrypted codes
incomprehensible to adults, insouciant to friends, and doomed to obsolescence. The internet
has turbocharged this cycle, turning slang into cultural currency traded across reels and clips,
on Instagram and Discord servers. Once upon a timeline, things were “on fleek”. Then came
“yeet” and “slay”. Before that, everything was “lit” and YOLO, miles above “mid”. “Skibidi”
came and went in the space of a meme. “Six-seven” has followed the same pattern of digital
migration. It appears to have sprouted from a 2024 rap track, ‘Doot Doot’ (6 7) by Skrilla,
before mutating through basketball fandom, mostly of LaMelo Ball, 6ft 7in — but of course
— and landing in an episode of South Park. Along the way, it also acquired a visual meme
code: Upturned palms, rising and falling in tandem.
The freedom of such coinages has always been in their ephemerality: A flare of rebellion
against the grammar police, a reminder that language, like adolescence, can be play —
elastic, irreverent and gloriously incomprehensible to those who pay the WiFi bill — before
maturing into something entirely mundane. The other surest way to kill a trend, of course, is
to have parents use it. Or worse, wear it. In the United States this Halloween, “six-seven”
costumes are reportedly gaining traction among parents, much to the agony of their offspring.
Because nothing says the death of cool quite like dad wearing it.

V. It can look like garbage and act like garbage but litter is something different – garbage placed
where it shouldn’t be. As popular as this activity is among us Indians we were aghast to learn
that a lady walking about outer London was fined £150 for it. All she had done was pour the
last of her coffee down a drain. She hadn’t even thrown her mug in. It was reusable. Nearer us,

in Singapore littering fines can go up to S$2,000 – and to S$10,000 beyond the third conviction.
If our governments went about fining litterers so liberally, the collection could put GST
revenues to shame.
Why are Indians so fond of littering? We see a choking river, we worsen its misery. We see a
pristine one, we introduce it to plastic bags, paper napkins, rubber chappals. Sometimes we
throw the half-eaten burger right next to a wastebin. My one chewing gum wrapper won’t make
a difference, our demon self whispers. Except it’s joined by a hundred, thousand, million others,
and it makes all the difference.
We loooove to holiday in Japan but guess what helps make it so holidayable? People carry their
trash home rather than spray it about. We cleaned our homes thoroughly on Diwali but spread
its detritus across our parks and streets. Cleaning all that is someone else’s job, we think. But
if we want to live in a clean society, we too have to stop doing the dirty.

X. The Sale of Goods Act establishes a foundational commercial framework by distinguishing
between two pivotal types of contractual terms: conditions and warranties. A condition is a
fundamental term central to the contract's identity, the breach of which entitles the aggrieved
party to treat the contract as repudiated, reject the goods, and claim damages. In contrast, a
warranty is a subsidiary or collateral promise, breach of which only grants a right to damages,
not termination. This distinction is critical as it dictates the available remedies, ensuring
proportionality between the breach's gravity and the legal recourse.
Regarding stipulations as to time, the Act provides clarity on contractual performance
deadlines. Unless a different intention is expressly stated or necessarily implied from the
contract's circumstances, time of payment is not deemed to be "of the essence." However, time
for delivery may be construed as a condition if the commercial context or explicit agreement
indicates its fundamental importance, allowing rejection for delayed performance.
The Act's most significant contribution lies in its implied conditions and warranties, which
operate as core statutory protections. These terms are automatically woven into every sales
contract unless explicitly excluded. Primarily, there is an implied condition on title: that the
seller has the legal right to sell the goods. Further, where goods are sold by description, there
is a condition that they will correspond materially with that description. Critically, goods must
be of satisfactory quality—considering their price, description, and durability—and be
reasonably fit for any particular purpose the buyer made known to the seller, implying reliance
on the seller's skill or judgment. Finally, in a sale by sample, implied conditions stipulate that
the bulk will correspond with the sample in quality, and that the buyer will have a reasonable
opportunity to compare the two, safeguarding against latent defects not apparent in the sample.
Collectively, these provisions create a balanced legal architecture, protecting buyers from
deficient performance while providing sellers with clear standards, thereby facilitating fair and
predictable commercial exchange.

judicial efficiency while balancing the interests of justice. Two significant provisions in this
regard are Plea Bargaining and the Summary Procedure for compoundable and non-
compoundable offences, both designed to expedite the resolution of specific categories of
cases.
Plea Bargaining, introduced under Chapter XXI-A (Sections 265A-265L), represents a
transformative departure from conventional adversarial litigation. This judicially supervised

against women or children below fourteen. The procedure is initiated by the accused filing an

compounding and summary trials allow the criminal justice system to allocate its resources

expedited settlements for less severe transgressions.

ecosystem sustained by a body of interpretive principles. These judicial doctrines, developed
over decades, serve as essential tools for navigating the complex interplay between different
constitutional mandates, legislative entries, and fundamental guarantees. They allow the
judiciary to perform its delicate role as the guardian of the constitutional scheme without

necessity to resolve apparent conflicts, whether between competing legislative powers of the
Union and the States, or between the state’s authority to make laws and the citizen’s inviolable

At the heart of this interpretive jurisprudence lies the need to balance federal architecture with
individual liberties. One key area involves assessing laws that appear to contradict foundational
freedoms granted by the Constitution. Here, the judiciary may examine whether such an archaic
law is permanently invalid or possesses a potential for future operation, a concept distinct from
total nullity. Similarly, in a federal system, disputes inevitably arise concerning which
legislature—Union or State—is competent to enact a particular law. To adjudicate such
disputes, courts often look beyond the apparent subject of a statute to its core purpose and
substantial effect, ensuring that legislatures operate within their constitutionally demarcated
spheres. This prevents legislative overreach where the form of a law masks a trespass into a
forbidden domain, a situation where the substance of the legislation is scrutinized against the
backdrop of the Seventh Schedule.
Furthermore, when a law enacted by a state legislature is challenged for purportedly affecting
matters beyond its territorial jurisdiction, the courts apply a principle to determine if a sufficient
connection exists between the state and the subject of the legislation. This ensures that state
laws having extra-territorial impact remain constitutionally sound. Ultimately, when two
constitutional provisions or statutory interpretations seem in tension, the guiding imperative is
to adopt a construction that reconciles them, preserving the integrity of the legal text and giving
effect to the holistic intent of the framers. Collectively, these doctrines embody the
constitutional ethos of equilibrium, ensuring a harmonious coexistence of power, liberty, and
federalism.

XIV. Public nuisance is a distinct legal doctrine addressing an unreasonable and substantial
interference with a right common to the general public, such as health, safety, peace, or
convenience. Unlike a private nuisance, which protects an individual’s enjoyment of land, a
public nuisance defends communal rights. Classic examples include obstructing a public
highway, polluting a river used by the community, maintaining a house of prostitution, or
creating a public health hazard. Its character as a wrong against the public means it is frequently
both a crime, prosecutable by the state, and a tort, allowing for civil redress.
A critical and defining element of public nuisance law is the stringent requirement for standing
to sue. Historically, only the state, acting through the Attorney General, could bring suit to
abate a public nuisance. This reflected the principle that a wrong to the public should be
rectified by the public’s representative. The modern rule, however, permits a private citizen to
file a civil action, but only upon demonstrating a “special injury.” This harm must be
qualitatively different in kind, not merely greater in degree, from the inconvenience suffered
by the general public. For instance, while all citizens may be delayed by an illegally blocked
road, a shop owner whose sole access is cut off, causing unique and severe economic losses,
suffers the requisite special injury to pursue a claim.
The remedies available correspond to the party bringing the action. The primary remedy sought
by the state is an injunction—a court order compelling the defendant to cease the offending
activity. Public authorities may also exercise their power of abatement, directly removing the
nuisance (e.g., clearing an obstruction). For the private plaintiff who successfully proves both
the public nuisance and a special injury, the available remedy is compensatory damages for
their distinct losses. Thus, public nuisance law operates on two tiers: one for the protection of
the collective welfare and another, more narrow path, for redressing exceptional harm to private
individuals arising from that public wrong.
